claims.text: Selecting Al as X in CrFeCoNiX promotes a more continuous protective oxide above 900 °C than selecting Si or Mn.
Selecting Al as X promotes a more coherent oxide scale than selecting Si or Mn.
Selecting Al as X produces a slower-growing oxide scale than selecting Si or Mn.
The improved oxidation behavior of the Al-containing alloy is attributable to formation of a dense alumina-based oxide.
Favorable elemental segregation in the Al-containing alloy minimizes oxide–substrate lattice mismatch and oxide growth stresses.
Reduced interfacial mismatch and growth stress prevent cracking and spallation of the oxide scale.
The proposed comparison applies to CrFeCoNiX alloys in single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution states, with X selected from Al, Si, and Mn.
Oxide-scale integrity is governed by continuity, substrate coherence, defect content, and residual stress.
Al preferentially segregates during high-temperature exposure.
Segregated Al forms a dense alumina-based oxide.
The alumina-based oxide has low oxygen diffusivity.
The alumina-based oxide has minimal volume-expansion mismatch with the alloy.
Low oxygen diffusivity and low expansion mismatch cause the alumina-based scale to grow slowly and remain adherent.
CrFeCoNi alloys containing Si or Mn form less stable, higher-stress oxide scales than the corresponding Al-containing alloy.
Si- or Mn-containing alloys have higher oxide growth rates and greater susceptibility to cracking or spallation than the Al-containing alloy.
The proposed behavior is expected during prolonged exposure above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive environments.
Processing history, grain size, and minor composition changes may alter the oxidation outcome.
Evidence supports the role of Al in forming more coherent protective oxide layers.
Quantitative differences in oxide growth kinetics and residual stress remain uncertain and may depend on environment and processing.
Failure of the Al-containing alloy to show significantly better coherence, slower growth, greater adhesion, and lower residual stress than both controls would falsify the proposed role of Al.
